tasks.text:
Every project review in our department begins with the same question: what actually went wrong? Last spring the team spent four weeks arguing about the budget, and it was that argument that delayed the launch. The budget itself was never the real problem. What the reviewers finally identified was a single missing test, a fault so small that nobody had considered it salient. It is this pattern, rather than any shortage of money, that explains most of our failures.
Since then we have changed the way we open a review. What we look for first is the crux of the problem, not the loudest complaint in the room. It was our new director who insisted on the rule, and her reasoning was simple. If a team cannot name the underlying cause in one sentence, it does not yet understand it. Trivial details are still recorded, but they are set aside; what receives attention is the decisive factor. The change has been substantial. Reviews that once consumed a whole afternoon now take under an hour, and the conclusions we reach are far more definitive.

tasks.text:
For almost a century the manuscript in the city museum was believed to have been written in 1420. That date is printed in every guidebook, and until recently nobody had tried to substantiate it. Last year a team from the university was reported to have found a second copy in a private collection. The second copy is thought to have been produced by the same workshop, yet its paper is clearly younger.
The old claim was quickly denounced by two historians, who pointed out that the earlier date had never been documented anywhere. Their objection is now widely cited. The museum, however, is said to have refused every new test, and its director is understood to have called the whole question unimportant.
Since then a small laboratory has been allowed to examine a single page. The results are believed to have corroborated the historians. The manuscript is now supposed to have been copied around 1560, more than a hundred years later than the label in the hall still claims. The museum has not corrected that label.

tasks.text:
Having worked on the same river project for three years, the planning group finally presented its report last month. Being aware of the public interest, the city published the whole document online the same evening.
The report comprises four parts. Having studied the older plans first, the authors decided to begin with history. Their account, drawing on maps from the last century, shows how the two districts on either bank slowly diverged. Being separated by the water and by a busy road, the two neighbourhoods developed almost independently.
The second part encompasses transport. Having counted the traffic for six months, the team argues that a new bridge would entail far higher costs than a ferry. The third part, being the shortest of all, deals with parks.
Having read every comment received in April, the council will vote in June. Officials say that, being a long-term plan, the project must survive several changes of government. Whatever is decided, the debate is expected to culminate in a public meeting at the end of the year.

tasks.text:
Our editor has one rule, and every new writer soon learns it: if a word can be omitted, omit it. She never explains the rule twice, and she does not need to. Her marks in the margin are short, and so are her comments.
Last week she returned my article with three lines crossed out. You have said this already, she wrote, so do not restate it. I had used four sentences where one would do. Having read her note, I condensed the whole paragraph and sent it back the same evening.
Good writers, she says, use substitution rather than repetition. If you have written the old report once, the second time write the old one. If a colleague says she enjoyed the meeting and you enjoyed it too, say so did I rather than repeating the entire sentence. English allows both forms, but the shorter one always sounds more natural.
Some students find this advice ambiguous, and I did too at first. Yet the principle is simple. Say it once, clearly; if the reader can supply the missing words, leave them out.

tasks.text:
The implementation of the new water regulation began in March. Its evaluation, however, will not take place until next year, and that delay has already attracted criticism.
The report identifies three problems. The first is the allocation of funds. The distribution of money between the districts followed the old classification of regions, and no justification for that decision appears in the documents. The second problem is supervision. The administration of the programme was divided between two offices, and the coordination of their work was weak from the very start.
The third problem concerns transparency. Public access to the figures required a written request, and the verification of those figures by an independent body never took place. According to the authors, the absence of accountability made any interpretation of the results almost impossible.
The recommendations themselves are short. They call for the integration of the two offices, the introduction of a single reporting standard, and the adaptation of the timetable to the real speed of the work. Compliance with that standard would be checked twice a year. The transformation, the authors admit, will be slow.
